mpas.news_summary:
The latest relevant report in the available information is **Operation Island Chief 2026**, a regional Pacific surveillance operation conducted **3–14 August 2026**. It covered about **27.5 million km²**, including the EEZs of 11 FFA members and adjacent high seas—not specifically the Phoenix Islands Protected Area.

The operation monitored more than 3,000 fishing vessels, identified **16 vessels of interest**, and resulted in **four vessels being detained or apprehended**. Authorities in **Kiribati, Palau and Papua New Guinea** detained or took vessels to port over suspected illegal fishing or fishing-licence breaches; reports identified Chinese and Indonesian vessels among them. The available reports do **not** say whether any of these incidents occurred in or near the Phoenix Islands Protected Area, or identify the 16 vessels. ([FFA](https://www.ffa.int/2026/08/operation-island-chief-identifies-16-vessels-of-interest-in-major-regional-surveillance-effort-against-illegal-fishing/); [The Manila Times](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/08/22/world/asia-oceania/chinese-indonesian-boats-detained-for-illegal-fishing/2409992))
mpas.rules_summary:
**The 2015–2020 PIPA Management Plan describes the whole protected area as closed to extraction, with an exception for designated artisanal fishing zones at Kanton to support the island’s community.** That means commercial fishing—including industrial tuna fishing—was prohibited under the plan, while limited local artisanal fishing was allowed in those zones. The plan also says PIPA’s Regulations 2008 provide the legal mandate for managing activities in the area.

That is the clearest official rule in the sources provided, but it is a **2015–2020 plan**, not confirmation of the rules currently in force. A 2021 news report says Kiribati announced it would reopen PIPA to commercial fishing; the material provided does not establish whether that change was formally approved or what current regulations apply. So I can’t confirm the present-day status or current no-take boundaries from these sources.

**Official sources**
- [Government of Kiribati, *PIPA Management Plan 2015–2020*](https://rris.biopama.org/sites/default/files/2021-04/PIPA-Management-Plan-2015-2020.pdf): describes full protection from extraction, except designated artisanal fishing zones at Kanton.
- [Government of Kiribati PIPA Implementation Office, *PIPA Visitors Guidelines*](https://www.melad.gov.ki/images/pipa/Permit_and_Guidelines/PIPA_Visitors_Guidelines.pdf): says visitors must follow PIPA fishing regulations and that harvesting resources requires a permit; it does not specify the current commercial-fishing rules.

**Latest relevant update:** A La Nación opinion article dated **November 14, 2026** says Costa Rica’s SINAC is reviewing a petition to declare the management plan for the Área Marina de Manejo del Bicentenario (AMMB) absolutely void. The article says longline fishing is allowed across most of the AMMB, with exceptions including a five-nautical-mile buffer around Isla del Coco National Park and two-mile zones around four seamounts.

The supplied sources **do not report a recent detention or enforcement action specifically at or near Isla del Coco**. They do describe radar monitoring around the island and regional concerns about illegal fishing, but the reported vessel interceptions and enforcement figures concern other protected areas, such as Panama’s Coiba and Colombia’s Malpelo and Gorgona.
mpas.rules_summary:
**Within Isla del Coco National Park, fishing of any kind is prohibited**—including sport and commercial fishing. The park’s restrictions also prohibit fishing boats from entering or being present in its marine area, which extends 12 nautical miles around the island. The official visitor brochure lists both restrictions. [Costa Rica tourism brochure, *Parque Nacional Isla del Coco*](https://www.visitcostarica.com/sites/default/files/legacy/pdf/7_PN%20Isla%20del%20Coco.pdf)

So the park is a **no-take area for fishing**. The available material describes one protected marine area around the island; it does not identify separate internal no-take zones.

The prohibition is consistent with a scientific paper citing Executive Decree No. 29834-MINAE, which says extraction of marine resources and commercial and industrial activities are banned within the park. [SciELO article](https://www.scielo.sa.cr/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S0034-77442012000800021)

**Nearby waters are different:** Global Fishing Watch describes the adjoining Seamounts Marine Management Area as allowing fishing by Costa Rican artisanal vessels only. That allowance applies to the adjacent management area, not the National Park. [Global Fishing Watch](https://globalfishingwatch.org/impacts/policy-compliance/protecting-cocos-island/)

### Latest reported developments

- **October 2, 2026 — Detentions and alleged abuse:** Human Rights Watch reported that U.S. forces intercepted and destroyed eight Ecuadorian fishing vessels between August 28 and September 16, detaining more than 140 of 160 crew members and allegedly abusing some. On September 10, a judge on San Cristóbal ordered 28 crew members released without charge. The report concerns maritime operations near Ecuador; the supplied information does not establish that all eight vessels were inside the Galápagos Marine Reserve.
- **August–September 2026 — Regional exercise:** Ecuador hosted **GALAPEX 2026**, a multinational exercise near the Galápagos focused on cooperation against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. The U.S. Coast Guard and partner nations took part in simulated vessel inspections and pursuit exercises.
- **March 2026 — Reserve impact study:** A report summarizing research published in *Marine Policy* said industrial fishing inside the Hermandad reserve fell by 88% soon after its establishment in January 2022. This is a research finding, not a new detention or enforcement action.

The available material does not provide a confirmed, recent detention of a foreign fishing vessel **inside** the Galápagos Marine Reserve. It does describe continuing concern about distant-water fleets operating near the reserve, but some claims—such as suspected nighttime incursions—are presented as suspicions rather than confirmed incidents.
mpas.rules_summary:
**Industrial fishing is prohibited inside the Galápagos Marine Reserve.** A fisheries analysis reports that, since the reserve was established in 1998, industrial fishing using hydraulic, mechanized, or technical gear has been prohibited there. It distinguishes the reserve from the surrounding Insular Exclusive Economic Zone, where industrial fishing occurs. [Responsible Seafood Advocate](https://www.globalseafood.org/advocate/fishing-effort-dynamics-around-the-galapagos-marine-reserve-as-described-by-automatic-identification-system-data/)

**Commercial fishing is not prohibited altogether:** the available sources say that regulated artisanal fishing by licensed local fishers is allowed. The Galápagos National Park Directorate describes rules covering fishing licences, permits, authorized gear, and fishing seasons. [Galápagos National Park Directorate](https://galapagos.gob.ec/iniciamos-la-construccion-del-nuevo-reglamento-de-pesca/)

**There are no-take areas**, but the information provided does not establish their current official boundaries or rules. A research summary describes some no-take zones within the reserve; for current locations, consult the official zoning map or regulations from the Galápagos National Park Directorate.

mpas.news_summary:
The latest reported developments are from **July 2026**:

- On **July 7**, Mexico’s environment ministry (Semarnat), through CONANP, said it was designing an inter-agency strategy to combat illegal fishing in Revillagigedo National Park. The plan includes technological monitoring and coordination with Profepa, Conapesca, the federal prosecutor’s office, the Navy and the foreign ministry.
- A **July 9 report** said satellite monitoring had identified vessels that allegedly switched off their Automatic Identification System to enter the protected area undetected. It also noted that fishing has been prohibited within the park since its designation as a protected area in 2017.
- Earlier, in **April 2025**, CONANP reportedly used Skylight and Global Fishing Watch to detect a vessel suspected of illegal fishing near Clarión Island.

The material describes surveillance and enforcement plans, but **does not report a recent vessel detention or seizure** in or near the park.
mpas.rules_summary:
Fishing is prohibited throughout the Revillagigedo National Park—not just industrial or commercial fishing, but recreational fishing as well. The park is therefore a **no-take area**; the available information does not describe separate internal no-take zones or fishing-permitted zones.

**Official-source caveat:** The cited materials report that the 2017 presidential decree bans fishing, but they do not include the decree’s text or a Mexican government webpage. The IUCN account describes the decree as banning fishing in the reserve and on the islands. mpas.rules_summary:
Hermandad is divided into two 30,000 km² zones:

- **No-take zone:** Extractive activities are prohibited.
- **Responsible-fishing zone:** Fishing is allowed, **except fishing with longlines (palangre)**.

mpas.news_summary:
The latest information provided (through September 2026) concerns **proposed fishing access and regulation—not reports of illegal fishing or vessel detentions inside or near Papahānaumokuākea**. No recent detention or confirmed illegal-fishing incident is reported in these sources.

- **June 11, 2026:** President Trump signed a proclamation seeking to allow U.S.-flagged commercial fishing in parts of Papahānaumokuākea, including the Mau and Ho‘omalu zones and areas beyond 50 nautical miles. The move was criticized by conservation groups; the supplied material does not establish whether fishing has begun there.
- **September 16, 2026:** The Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council discussed fishing access and management for the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands and Papahānaumokuākea sanctuary, but deferred action on relevant regulations. It noted that other federal requirements—such as permits, reporting, catch limits, gear rules, monitoring and protected-species measures—would still apply.
- **Background:** One source reports that commercial fishing was briefly allowed in part of Papahānaumokuākea in an earlier period and cites NOAA data showing 7,800 sharks caught as bycatch in the last year fishing was allowed there. This is not a report of illegal fishing or a recent vessel detention.

**Bottom line:** The supplied news points to a contested effort to expand commercial fishing access, but it contains no confirmed recent report of illegal fishing or vessel detentions in or near the monument.
mpas.rules_summary:
**Yes—industrial/commercial fishing is prohibited.** NOAA’s sanctuary regulations prohibit commercial fishing and possession of commercial fishing gear unless it is stowed and unavailable for immediate use. The monument’s broader rules also prohibit taking or disturbing resources unless authorized by a monument permit. [NOAA sanctuary regulations](https://sanctuaries.noaa.gov/papahanaumokuakea/management/regulations.html); [NOAA fishing-impact overview](https://sanctuaries.noaa.gov/science/sentinel-site-program/papahanaumokuakea/fishing-impacts.html).

**There are no-take protections across the monument, but fishing rules differ in the newly designated outer sanctuary area.** In the monument, fishing is generally prohibited unless permitted. In the Outer Sanctuary Zone—waters from 50 nautical miles to the U.S. EEZ boundary west of 163° W—non-commercial fishing may be allowed under applicable federal rules, provided the catch does not enter commerce; it requires authorization. Commercial fishing remains prohibited there. [NOAA sanctuary regulations](https://sanctuaries.noaa.gov/papahanaumokuakea/management/regulations.html).

So, describing the *entire* area as strictly no-take without qualification would miss the outer-zone allowance for authorized non-commercial fishing.

mpas.mpa_name: Cordillera de Coiba - Área de Recursos Manejados
mpas.news_summary:
**Latest reported incident:** On **July 12, 2026**, Panama’s Environment Ministry intercepted a sport-fishing yacht operating without authorization in Coiba National Park and ordered it to leave the protected area. The available report does not say the yacht was detained. ([MiAmbiente](https://miambiente.gob.pa/miambiente-realiza-patrullajes-intensivos-en-la-zona-especial-marina-del-parque-nacional-coiba/); [Telemetro](https://www.telemetro.com/nacionales/miambiente-detecta-yate-pesca-deportiva-autorizacion-coiba-n6084982))

Other recent cases include a **longliner held on February 5, 2026**, after allegedly spending 48 hours in the Cordillera de Coiba protected area; it was taken to Puerto Mutis. In January 2025, authorities detected **16 commercial longliners** in the area, in what they described as Panama’s largest operation against illegal fishing in a marine protected area.

A July 2026 Mongabay follow-up reports that the 2025 cases involved **21 Panamanian-owned vessels**. ARAP fined 13, dismissed seven cases, and reduced many fines on appeal; the Environment Ministry’s cases remained under appeal. Vessel owners disputed that they had fished inside the protected area, and agencies rejected criticism of how the cases were handled.
mpas.rules_summary:
**Fishing is restricted by zone; it is not prohibited throughout the entire area.**

- **Zone 1 is a no-extraction marine reserve.** MiAmbiente says it covers about two-thirds of the water area and the entire seabed, and is for total protection and non-extraction of natural resources. Its plan prohibits commercial and sport fishing from boats, as well as listed fishing methods including trawls, nets, longlines, and other gear. [MiAmbiente: fishing licenses under the management plan](https://miambiente.gob.pa/licencias-de-pesca-para-caneros-se-realizaran-bajo-las-normas-establecidas-en-el-plan-de-manejo-de-la-zona-marina-protegida-de-coiba/); [Zone 1 summary of the management plan](https://map.navigatormap.org/site-detail?site_id=20418).
- **Zone 2 allows limited fishing under the plan’s rules.** MiAmbiente describes it as about 22,626 km² and says fishing with rod and line (“cañeros”) is subject to specific requirements. Thus, the available official information does **not** support saying that all commercial fishing is banned across the whole managed area. [MiAmbiente](https://miambiente.gob.pa/licencias-de-pesca-para-caneros-se-realizaran-bajo-las-normas-establecidas-en-el-plan-de-manejo-de-la-zona-marina-protegida-de-coiba/).
- MiAmbiente also states that restrictions on specified fishing gear remain in force throughout the area under Executive Decree 138 of June 8, 2021. [MiAmbiente: fishing must follow strict sustainability rules](https://miambiente.gob.pa/navarro-la-pesca-tiene-que-darse-bajo-normas-estrictas-de-sostenibilidad/).

**Bottom line:** There is a substantial no-take zone—Zone 1—but the supplied sources describe regulated fishing in Zone 2. The cited MiAmbiente pages are official; the detailed Zone 1 summary is hosted by ProtectedSeas Navigator, not an official government site.

mpa_rules.answer:
**The 2015–2020 PIPA Management Plan describes the whole protected area as closed to extraction, with an exception for designated artisanal fishing zones at Kanton to support the island’s community.** That means commercial fishing—including industrial tuna fishing—was prohibited under the plan, while limited local artisanal fishing was allowed in those zones. The plan also says PIPA’s Regulations 2008 provide the legal mandate for managing activities in the area.

That is the clearest official rule in the sources provided, but it is a **2015–2020 plan**, not confirmation of the rules currently in force. A 2021 news report says Kiribati announced it would reopen PIPA to commercial fishing; the material provided does not establish whether that change was formally approved or what current regulations apply. So I can’t confirm the present-day status or current no-take boundaries from these sources.

**Official sources**
- [Government of Kiribati, *PIPA Management Plan 2015–2020*](https://rris.biopama.org/sites/default/files/2021-04/PIPA-Management-Plan-2015-2020.pdf): describes full protection from extraction, except designated artisanal fishing zones at Kanton.
- [Government of Kiribati PIPA Implementation Office, *PIPA Visitors Guidelines*](https://www.melad.gov.ki/images/pipa/Permit_and_Guidelines/PIPA_Visitors_Guidelines.pdf): says visitors must follow PIPA fishing regulations and that harvesting resources requires a permit; it does not specify the current commercial-fishing rules.

# EASTERN STAR — high risk lead
**Summary:** The EASTERN STAR, a Nauru-flagged fishing vessel, was detected in the Phoenix Islands Protected Area with its AIS switched off for 327 hours and engaged in apparent fishing. The vessel has a history of 45 tracking gaps in the past 12 months and has used multiple flags and names.
## What happened
* 2026-06-01T23:45:00.000Z: Apparent fishing event started
* 2026-06-04T19:36:29.000Z: Apparent fishing event started inside Phoenix Islands Protected Area
* 2026-06-04T21:54:10.000Z: AIS tracking switched off
* 2026-06-18T13:03:51.000Z: AIS tracking switched back on
## Why it matters
The EASTERN STAR's actions raised concerns due to its high risk score of 100, driven by factors such as switching off its AIS 1 time in a protected area, a long dark period of 327 hours, and engaging in apparent fishing inside the protected area. The vessel also met or loitered with another vessel at sea, potentially transferring catch, and has a history of using multiple flags and names.
## Vessel background
The EASTERN STAR is a fishing vessel flagged in Nauru, with an IMO number of 8996097 and MMSI 544113120. It has used multiple names (EASTERN STAR, ATUN STA, EASTERNSTAR) and flags (NRU, PNG, VUT). In the past 12 months, it had 45 tracking gaps, 232 apparent fishing events, 12 encounters, and 191 loitering events. It is authorized by FFA and WCPFC.
## What public sources say
The available information does not report EASTERN STAR for IUU fishing, detention, or fines [1]. The Phoenix Islands Protected Area was designated as a "no-take" zone in 2015, but a 2021 news report suggests Kiribati announced it would reopen PIPA to commercial fishing [5].
## What we don't know
None listed.
## Suggested next steps
1. Investigate the reason for the 327-hour tracking gap and verify the vessel's activities during that period.
2. Review the vessel's authorization records with FFA and WCPFC to ensure compliance with regulations.
3. Analyze the vessel's encounters and loitering events to determine if they were related to potential catch transfers or other suspicious activities.

mpa_rules.answer:
**The 2015–2020 PIPA Management Plan describes the whole protected area as closed to extraction, with an exception for designated artisanal fishing zones at Kanton to support the island’s community.** That means commercial fishing—including industrial tuna fishing—was prohibited under the plan, while limited local artisanal fishing was allowed in those zones. The plan also says PIPA’s Regulations 2008 provide the legal mandate for managing activities in the area.

That is the clearest official rule in the sources provided, but it is a **2015–2020 plan**, not confirmation of the rules currently in force. A 2021 news report says Kiribati announced it would reopen PIPA to commercial fishing; the material provided does not establish whether that change was formally approved or what current regulations apply. So I can’t confirm the present-day status or current no-take boundaries from these sources.

**Official sources**
- [Government of Kiribati, *PIPA Management Plan 2015–2020*](https://rris.biopama.org/sites/default/files/2021-04/PIPA-Management-Plan-2015-2020.pdf): describes full protection from extraction, except designated artisanal fishing zones at Kanton.
- [Government of Kiribati PIPA Implementation Office, *PIPA Visitors Guidelines*](https://www.melad.gov.ki/images/pipa/Permit_and_Guidelines/PIPA_Visitors_Guidelines.pdf): says visitors must follow PIPA fishing regulations and that harvesting resources requires a permit; it does not specify the current commercial-fishing rules.

mpa_rules.answer:
**The 2015–2020 PIPA Management Plan describes the whole protected area as closed to extraction, with an exception for designated artisanal fishing zones at Kanton to support the island’s community.** That means commercial fishing—including industrial tuna fishing—was prohibited under the plan, while limited local artisanal fishing was allowed in those zones. The plan also says PIPA’s Regulations 2008 provide the legal mandate for managing activities in the area.

That is the clearest official rule in the sources provided, but it is a **2015–2020 plan**, not confirmation of the rules currently in force. A 2021 news report says Kiribati announced it would reopen PIPA to commercial fishing; the material provided does not establish whether that change was formally approved or what current regulations apply. So I can’t confirm the present-day status or current no-take boundaries from these sources.

**Official sources**
- [Government of Kiribati, *PIPA Management Plan 2015–2020*](https://rris.biopama.org/sites/default/files/2021-04/PIPA-Management-Plan-2015-2020.pdf): describes full protection from extraction, except designated artisanal fishing zones at Kanton.
- [Government of Kiribati PIPA Implementation Office, *PIPA Visitors Guidelines*](https://www.melad.gov.ki/images/pipa/Permit_and_Guidelines/PIPA_Visitors_Guidelines.pdf): says visitors must follow PIPA fishing regulations and that harvesting resources requires a permit; it does not specify the current commercial-fishing rules.

**The available reports link FONG KUO FISHERIES to IUU fishing, but do not establish that the company itself was sanctioned or used forced labour.**

- **IUU fishing:** Greenpeace’s *Government Failure and Illegal, Abusive and Criminal Fisheries Made in Taiwan* describes illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing in Taiwan’s fleet and identifies **Fong Chun Formosa Fishery** as a dominant company. Greenpeace Southeast Asia’s report on Taiwan’s tuna suppliers says migrant fishers described IUU practices on at least two vessels confirmed to be supplying to **Fong Chun Formosa (FCF)**.
- **Forced labour:** The Greenpeace Southeast Asia report discusses forced-labour allegations in Taiwan’s distant-water fisheries and vessels supplying FCF. The supplied excerpt does not establish that FCF itself directly employed workers under forced-labour conditions.

The sources name **Fong Chun Formosa Fishery/FCF**, not “FONG KUO FISHERIES.” The information provided does not confirm that those names refer to the same company, so the links should not be attributed to FONG KUO without further verification.

# FONG KUO NO.688 — high risk lead
**Summary:** The FONG KUO NO.688, a Taiwan-flagged tuna purse seiner, was apparently involved in multiple fishing events within the Phoenix Islands Protected Area, a protected marine reserve, and has a history of tracking gaps and possible IUU fishing links. Its activities raise concerns about potential illegal fishing in a protected area.
## What happened
* 2026-06-01T20:07:56.000Z: Started apparent fishing 30.8 hours before a 285-hour tracking gap
* 2026-06-03T05:53:18.000Z: Tracking gap began in Phoenix Islands Protected Area
* 2026-06-15T03:02:49.000Z: Tracking gap ended
* 2026-06-15T04:07:09.000Z: Started apparent fishing 1.1 hours after tracking gap ended
* 2026-07-03T07:37:37.000Z: Started apparent fishing inside Phoenix Islands Protected Area
## Why it matters
The vessel's risk score is 100 due to multiple factors, including: switching off tracking 1 time in a protected area, a longest dark period of 285 hours, 7 apparent fishing events inside the protected area, and a history of 20 tracking gaps in the previous 12 months. It also had a possible catch transfer and has used multiple flags and names.
## Vessel background
The FONG KUO NO.688 is a tuna purse seiner flagged in Taiwan, with IMO 9764271 and MMSI 416253900. It is owned by FONG KUO FISHERIES or TRANS PACIFIC JOURNEY PNG, and has used the name KWILA888. In the 12 months prior to the incident, it had 20 tracking gaps, 87 apparent fishing events, 7 encounters, and 9 port visits.
## What public sources say
The vessel is listed as a tuna purse seiner by the WCPFC [2]. Greenpeace reports that Fong Chun Formosa Fishery (possibly linked to FONG KUO FISHERIES) has been associated with IUU fishing practices [5][6]. The Phoenix Islands Protected Area was closed to commercial fishing under the 2015-2020 management plan, except for designated artisanal fishing zones [10].
## What we don't know
There are no unknowns listed for this vessel.
## Suggested next steps
1. Investigate the vessel's activities before and after the tracking gap to determine if it was fishing illegally.
2. Verify the link between FONG KUO FISHERIES and Fong Chun Formosa Fishery to assess potential IUU fishing connections.
3. Check if the vessel's activities comply with current regulations in the Phoenix Islands Protected Area.

mpa_rules.answer:
**Within Isla del Coco National Park, fishing of any kind is prohibited**—including sport and commercial fishing. The park’s restrictions also prohibit fishing boats from entering or being present in its marine area, which extends 12 nautical miles around the island. The official visitor brochure lists both restrictions. [Costa Rica tourism brochure, *Parque Nacional Isla del Coco*](https://www.visitcostarica.com/sites/default/files/legacy/pdf/7_PN%20Isla%20del%20Coco.pdf)

So the park is a **no-take area for fishing**. The available material describes one protected marine area around the island; it does not identify separate internal no-take zones.

The prohibition is consistent with a scientific paper citing Executive Decree No. 29834-MINAE, which says extraction of marine resources and commercial and industrial activities are banned within the park. [SciELO article](https://www.scielo.sa.cr/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S0034-77442012000800021)

**Nearby waters are different:** Global Fishing Watch describes the adjoining Seamounts Marine Management Area as allowing fishing by Costa Rican artisanal vessels only. That allowance applies to the adjacent management area, not the National Park. [Global Fishing Watch](https://globalfishingwatch.org/impacts/policy-compliance/protecting-cocos-island/)

# F/V BELLE RIVE — high risk lead
**Summary:** The F/V BELLE RIVE, a fishing vessel flagged in Panama, was apparently involved in a prolonged tracking gap within the Isla del Coco National Park, a protected area. The vessel's actions during this period raise concerns due to the park's strict no-take policy for fishing.
## What happened
* 2026-04-28T10:29:38.000Z: The F/V BELLE RIVE's AIS tracking was apparently switched off.
* 2026-06-01T15:20:33.000Z: The F/V BELLE RIVE's AIS tracking resumed.
## Why it matters
The F/V BELLE RIVE's 820.85-hour tracking gap within the Isla del Coco National Park is concerning because the park prohibits all fishing activities. The vessel's actions during this period, including moving about 1002 km while tracking was off, suggest potential non-compliance with these regulations. The vessel has a history of 6 tracking gaps in the previous 12 months, and its use of multiple flags and names raises additional concerns. One web source links the vessel to potential illegal fishing, sanctions, or detentions [1].
## Vessel background
The F/V BELLE RIVE is identified by its IMO number 9679622 and MMSI 352999958. It is flagged in Panama but has also been associated with Mauritius. The vessel is owned by SAPMER SOCIETE ANONYME DE PECHE MALGACHE ET REUNIONNAISE, a company based in Réunion. In the 12 months prior to the incident, the vessel had 6 tracking gaps, 52 fishing events, and 12 port visits. The vessel's gear type is listed as TUNA_PURSE_SEINES, and it is authorized by the IOTC.
## What public sources say
The available reports do not confirm any instances of IUU fishing, sanctions, detentions, or fines for the F/V BELLE RIVE [1]. However, the vessel's owner, SAPMER, is described as having sustainable fishing practices, with certifications such as Friend of the Sea since 2012 [5]. Isla del Coco National Park has strict regulations, including a prohibition on fishing and the presence of fishing boats within its 12 nautical mile marine area [9].
## What we don't know
There are no unknowns listed for this investigation.
## Suggested next steps
1. Investigate the cause of the F/V BELLE RIVE's prolonged tracking gap within the Isla del Coco National Park.
2. Review the vessel's fishing activities and port visits in the 12 months prior to the incident to identify any patterns or potential non-compliance.
3. Examine the ownership and management structure of SAPMER SOCIETE ANONYME DE PECHE MALGACHE ET REUNIONNAISE to assess potential risks or links to IUU fishing.

**Industrial fishing is prohibited inside the Galápagos Marine Reserve.** A fisheries analysis reports that, since the reserve was established in 1998, industrial fishing using hydraulic, mechanized, or technical gear has been prohibited there. It distinguishes the reserve from the surrounding Insular Exclusive Economic Zone, where industrial fishing occurs. [Responsible Seafood Advocate](https://www.globalseafood.org/advocate/fishing-effort-dynamics-around-the-galapagos-marine-reserve-as-described-by-automatic-identification-system-data/)

**Commercial fishing is not prohibited altogether:** the available sources say that regulated artisanal fishing by licensed local fishers is allowed. The Galápagos National Park Directorate describes rules covering fishing licences, permits, authorized gear, and fishing seasons. [Galápagos National Park Directorate](https://galapagos.gob.ec/iniciamos-la-construccion-del-nuevo-reglamento-de-pesca/)

**There are no-take areas**, but the information provided does not establish their current official boundaries or rules. A research summary describes some no-take zones within the reserve; for current locations, consult the official zoning map or regulations from the Galápagos National Park Directorate.

# JUAN PABLO II — high risk lead
**Summary:** The JUAN PABLO II, a Panamanian-flagged fishing vessel, appears to have switched off its AIS tracking device while inside the Galápagos Marine Reserve, raising concerns about potential illegal activity. The vessel's 1133-hour tracking gap and significant movement during this period contribute to its high risk score.
## What happened
* 2026-06-04T21:42:13.000Z: Visited PANAMA ANCHORAGE PACIFIC
* 2026-06-07T22:22:43.000Z: Departed PANAMA ANCHORAGE PACIFIC
* 2026-06-10T11:31:08.000Z: AIS tracking switched off in Galápagos Marine Reserve
* 2026-07-27T16:52:23.000Z: AIS tracking resumed
* 2026-07-29T11:40:17.000Z: Visited PAITA

## Why it matters
The vessel's risk score is 70 due to several factors: it turned off its AIS tracking device once while in the Galápagos Marine Reserve, had a prolonged dark period of 1133 hours, moved approximately 1222 km during the tracking gap, has a history of 4 tracking gaps in the previous 12 months, and has been linked to potential illegal fishing or sanctions by at least one web source.

## Vessel background
The JUAN PABLO II is identified as a fishing vessel with IMO 9831189, MMSI 352001025, and callsign HO6883, flagged in Panama. It is authorized by IATTC and has been involved in 15 port visits in the last 12 months. The vessel has a history of 4 tracking gaps in the previous 12 months.

## What public sources say
No reports directly link the JUAN PABLO II (IMO 9831189, MMSI 352001025) to IUU fishing, sanctions, detentions, or fines. However, sources confirm it is a fishing vessel [1][2]. Industrial fishing is prohibited inside the Galápagos Marine Reserve, but regulated artisanal fishing is allowed [5][6].

## What we don't know

## Suggested next steps
1. Investigate the vessel's activities during the 1133-hour tracking gap to determine if it was engaged in fishing or other illicit activities.
2. Review the vessel's authorization and compliance with IATTC regulations.
3. Examine the vessel's port visits and cargo handling to identify potential patterns or anomalies.

mpa_rules.answer:
Fishing is prohibited throughout the Revillagigedo National Park—not just industrial or commercial fishing, but recreational fishing as well. The park is therefore a **no-take area**; the available information does not describe separate internal no-take zones or fishing-permitted zones.

**Official-source caveat:** The cited materials report that the 2017 presidential decree bans fishing, but they do not include the decree’s text or a Mexican government webpage. The IUCN account describes the decree as banning fishing in the reserve and on the islands. ProtectedSeas lists park rules prohibiting hunting and fishing, while pointing to the decree and 2019 management plan. These support the park-wide ban, but are not themselves Mexican government sources.

# DONA TERE — high risk lead
**Summary:** The DONA TERE, a Mexican-flagged fishing vessel, was apparently involved in suspicious activity within the Revillagigedo National Park, a protected area, with its AIS tracking switched off for an extended period. The vessel has a history of similar behavior, raising concerns about potential illegal fishing.
## What happened
* 2026-08-14T00:59:18.000Z: AIS tracking gap started
* 2026-08-31T19:37:28.000Z: AIS tracking gap ended
## Why it matters
The vessel's AIS was switched off 1 time in a protected area, it had a long dark period of 427 hours, moved about 647 km while tracking was off, met or loitered with another vessel at sea, has used multiple names, and has a repeat pattern of 7 tracking gaps in the previous 12 months, contributing to its high risk score of 70.
## Vessel background
The DONA TERE is a Mexican-flagged fishing vessel with MMSI 345080900 and IMO 9685592. It is owned by PESCA AZTECA and PINSA PESCADOS INDUSTRIALIZADOS. In the 12 months prior to the incident, it had 7 AIS gaps, 37 fishing events, 0 encounters, 47 loitering events, and 9 port visits.
## What public sources say
The vessel is identified as a Mexican-flag fishing vessel by various sources, including Maritime Optima, Voyage Radar, and VesselFinder [1][2][3]. No reports linking DONA TERE to IUU fishing, sanctions, detention, or fines were found. Pesca Azteca, one of the vessel's owners, was involved in a 2009 U.S. fishing-law case regarding unlawful fishing in the U.S. exclusive economic zone, but the case's outcome is not provided [5].
## What we don't know
No unknowns are listed for this case.
## Suggested next steps
1. Investigate the vessel's activity during the AIS gap to determine if it was fishing within the protected area.
2. Review the vessel's past 7 AIS gaps in the previous 12 months to identify any patterns or potential illegal activity.
3. Examine the encounter or loitering event with another vessel at sea to assess if it was related to a potential catch transfer or other suspicious activity.

# MAZPESCA 2 — medium risk lead
**Summary:** The Mexican-flagged fishing vessel MAZPESCA 2 was apparently involved in suspicious activity within the Revillagigedo National Park, a protected area, with its AIS tracking switched off for 52 hours. The vessel's history shows a pattern of 9 tracking gaps in the previous 12 months, contributing to a medium risk score.
## What happened
* 2026-06-25T19:15:36.000Z: Started fishing
* 2026-06-26T01:54:26.000Z: AIS tracking switched off
* 2026-06-28T06:23:12.000Z: AIS tracking switched back on
## Why it matters
The vessel's AIS was switched off for 52 hours while within the Revillagigedo National Park, a protected area where fishing is prohibited. The vessel moved about 494 km during this period, suggesting it was actively fishing or transiting. The vessel has a history of 9 tracking gaps in the previous 12 months, indicating a possible pattern of behavior to evade detection. The vessel also met or loitered with another vessel at sea, potentially indicating a catch transfer.
## Vessel background
The vessel MAZPESCA 2 is a Mexican-flagged fishing vessel (MMSI 345080022, IMO 7435266) owned by MAZPESCA. It has been identified using AIS and has a history of fishing activity. In the 12 months prior to the incident, it had 9 tracking gaps, 34 fishing events, 0 encounters, 32 loitering events, and 7 port visits. The vessel has used multiple names: MAZPESCA2 and MAZPESCA 2.
## What public sources say
No relevant public reports were found linking MAZPESCA 2 or its owner, MAZPESCA, to IUU fishing, sanctions, detention, or fines [5][7]. The Revillagigedo National Park is a no-take area, with all types of fishing prohibited since November 2017 [10][11].
## What we don't know
There are no unknowns listed for this case.
## Suggested next steps
1. Verify the vessel's AIS data to confirm the tracking gap and its location within the protected area.
2. Investigate the vessel's ownership and management structure to identify potential links to IUU fishing or other illicit activities.
3. Review the vessel's fishing authorizations and permits to determine if it was authorized to fish in the area.

# DONA ROGE — medium risk lead
**Summary:** The DONA ROGE, an Ecuadorian-flagged fishing vessel, was apparently involved in a prolonged tracking gap within the Galápagos Marine Reserve, raising concerns about potential illegal activity. The vessel's history includes multiple tracking gaps and fishing activities in the region.
## What happened
* 2026-05-30T02:54:00.000Z: Started loitering and fishing activities near the Galápagos Marine Reserve
* 2026-06-02T15:33:02.000Z: AIS tracking switched off, beginning a 992.87-hour gap
* 2026-07-14T00:24:59.000Z: AIS tracking resumed
* 2026-07-16T21:14:06.000Z: Visited the port of MANTA

## Why it matters
The DONA ROGE's risk score is 60 due to its prolonged tracking gap (993 hours) within the Galápagos Marine Reserve, a history of 9 tracking gaps in the previous 12 months, and movement of approximately 997 km while tracking was off. The vessel has also used multiple names (DONAROGE, DONA ROGE).

## Vessel background
The DONA ROGE is identified by its IMO number 7005279, MMSI 735057685, and callsign HC4301. It is flagged in Ecuador and owned by PESQUERA DONA ROGE and IBEROAMERICANA PESQUERA. The vessel is authorized to fish by IATTC and SPRFMO. In the past 12 months, it has had 9 tracking gaps, 100 fishing events, 1 encounter, 120 loitering events, and 12 port visits.

## What public sources say
No relevant public reports were found directly linking the DONA ROGE or its owners to IUU fishing, sanctions, or forced labor. Industrial fishing is prohibited within the Galápagos Marine Reserve, but regulated artisanal fishing by licensed local fishers is allowed [9]. The Galápagos National Park Directorate regulates fishing licenses, permits, and gear [10].

## What we don't know

## Suggested next steps
1. Investigate the cause of the prolonged AIS tracking gap and verify the vessel's activities during that period.
2. Review the vessel's fishing licenses and permits to ensure compliance with Galápagos Marine Reserve regulations.
3. Examine the vessel's ownership structure and check for any potential links to IUU fishing or labor abuse.

Hermandad is divided into two 30,000 km² zones:

- **No-take zone:** Extractive activities are prohibited.
- **Responsible-fishing zone:** Fishing is allowed, **except fishing with longlines (palangre)**.

So, it is not accurate to say that all commercial fishing is prohibited throughout Hermandad: fishing is expressly allowed in the responsible-fishing zone, subject to the longline ban. The available sources do not specify whether industrial fishing, as distinct from other fishing, is separately prohibited there.

# MARIA DE GRACIA — medium risk lead
**Summary:** The Ecuadorian-flagged fishing vessel MARIA DE GRACIA was detected loitering in the Hermandad - Reserva Marina protected area before switching off its AIS tracking for 171 hours. Its owner, ATUN TROPICAL ATUNTRO, has not been linked to any specific IUU fishing or sanctions reports.
## What happened
* 2026-07-30T09:57:33.000Z: Loitering detected in Hermandad - Reserva Marina for 1.01 hours
* 2026-07-30T10:58:10.000Z: AIS tracking switched off, resulting in a 171-hour gap
* 2026-08-06T14:03:38.000Z: AIS tracking resumed
## Why it matters
The vessel's risk score is 60 due to: 
- Switching off AIS tracking once in a protected area
- A longest dark period lasting 171 hours (over 3 days)
- Loitering with another vessel at sea, suggesting a possible catch transfer
- A repeat pattern of 7 tracking gaps in the previous 12 months
## Vessel background
MARIA DE GRACIA is an Ecuadorian-flagged fishing vessel (MMSI: 735057663, IMO: 7369754) owned by ATUN TROPICAL ATUNTRO. In the 12 months prior to the incident, it had 7 tracking gaps, 1 fishing event, 0 encounters, 3 loitering events, and 8 port visits.
## What public sources say
The available information does not establish that MARIA DE GRACIA has been reported for IUU fishing, sanctions, detention, or fines [1]. Hermandad - Reserva Marina has a 'no-take' zone where extractive activities are prohibited and a 'responsible-fishing' zone where fishing is allowed, except with longlines [9][10].
## What we don't know
None listed.
## Suggested next steps
1. Investigate the reason for the 171-hour AIS tracking gap.
2. Review any available data on the vessel's activities during the tracking gap.
3. Check for any potential encounters or interactions with other vessels during the loitering event.

mpa_rules.answer:
Hermandad is divided into two 30,000 km² zones:

- **No-take zone:** Extractive activities are prohibited.
- **Responsible-fishing zone:** Fishing is allowed, **except fishing with longlines (palangre)**.

So, it is not accurate to say that all commercial fishing is prohibited throughout Hermandad: fishing is expressly allowed in the responsible-fishing zone, subject to the longline ban. The available sources do not specify whether industrial fishing, as distinct from other fishing, is separately prohibited there.

# CAP.DANNY B — medium risk lead
**Summary:** The Ecuador-flagged fishing vessel CAP.DANNY B was apparently involved in a 391.51-hour tracking gap within the Hermandad - Reserva Marina protected area, raising concerns due to its history of similar incidents and other risk factors. The vessel's risk score is 60, indicating a medium risk level.
## What happened
* 2026-07-21T01:40:32.000Z: Tracking gap started
* 2026-08-06T09:11:21.000Z: Tracking gap ended
## Why it matters
The vessel's risk score is 60 due to several factors: it turned off its AIS tracking once in a protected area, had a long dark period of 392 hours, moved about 174 km while tracking was off, used multiple names, and had a repeat pattern of 3 tracking gaps in the previous 12 months.
## Vessel background
The CAP.DANNY B is identified by its IMO number 7015121, MMSI 735058922, and callsign HC5250. It is flagged in Ecuador and owned by B B TUNE SUPPLIERS, also based in Ecuador. The vessel is authorized to fish by IATTC and SPRFMO. In the 12 months prior to the incident, it had 3 tracking gaps, 0 fishing events, 0 encounters, 3 loitering events, and 3 port visits.
## What public sources say
No relevant public reports were found directly linking CAP.DANNY B to IUU fishing or other violations. However, reports discuss general fishing laws and policies [1]. There are also reports linking Taiwanese distant water fishing vessels and Bumble Bee canned tuna products to alleged forced labor practices, but these do not directly mention B B TUNE SUPPLIERS [5][6][8].
## What we don't know
There are no unknowns listed for this case.
## Suggested next steps
1. Investigate the cause of the 391.51-hour tracking gap and the vessel's activities during that time.
2. Review the vessel's previous tracking gaps and loitering events to identify any patterns or potential illegal activities.
3. Examine the vessel's port visits and fishing authorizations to ensure compliance with relevant regulations.

mpa_rules.answer:
Hermandad is divided into two 30,000 km² zones:

- **No-take zone:** Extractive activities are prohibited.
- **Responsible-fishing zone:** Fishing is allowed, **except fishing with longlines (palangre)**.

So, it is not accurate to say that all commercial fishing is prohibited throughout Hermandad: fishing is expressly allowed in the responsible-fishing zone, subject to the longline ban. The available sources do not specify whether industrial fishing, as distinct from other fishing, is separately prohibited there.

**Sources:** Ecuador’s Executive Decree and its zoning are summarized by [Galápagos Conservancy](https://www.galapagos.org/newsroom/timeline-the-expansion-of-the-galapagos-marine-reserve/) and [WildAid](https://wildaid.org/historic-decree-creates-a-new-marine-reserve-reserva-marina-de-hermandad-near-the-galapagos-islands-to-protect-a-massive-swimway-for-threatened-o/). These are not the decree itself; the supplied information also identifies the subsequent boundary instrument as Ministerial Agreement MAATE-2022-041, published in Ecuador’s Official Register.

# LA AHIJADA — medium risk lead
**Summary:** LA AHIJADA, an Ecuadorian-flagged fishing vessel, apparently turned off its AIS tracking in the Galápagos Marine Reserve for 1466 hours, moving 1253 km while dark. The vessel has a history of 7 tracking gaps in the past 12 months.
## What happened
* 2026-06-15T01:20:51.000Z: AIS tracking gap started
* 2026-08-15T03:24:25.000Z: AIS tracking gap ended, lasting 1466 hours
## Why it matters
The vessel's AIS was switched off 1 time in the Galápagos Marine Reserve, it had a long dark period of 1466 hours (3+ days), moved about 1253 km while tracking was off, and has a repeat pattern of 7 tracking gaps in the previous 12 months, indicating a potential risk of IUU fishing.
## Vessel background
LA AHIJADA is an Ecuadorian-flagged fishing vessel (MMSI 735055123, callsign HC4047) authorized by SPRFMO. It has been involved in fishing activities and has a history of 134 fishing events, 184 loitering events, and 10 port visits in the past 12 months. Its owner is unknown.
## What public sources say
No relevant public reports were found identifying LA AHIJADA as involved in IUU fishing, sanctions, detention, or fines [2]. Industrial fishing is prohibited inside the Galápagos Marine Reserve, but regulated artisanal fishing by licensed local fishers is allowed [5][6].
## What we don't know
None listed.
## Suggested next steps
1. Investigate the cause of the 1466-hour AIS tracking gap.
2. Review the vessel's fishing activities and loitering events in the Galápagos Marine Reserve.
3. Check if LA AHIJADA has any authorized fishing permits for the Galápagos Marine Reserve.

mpa_rules.answer:
**Yes—industrial/commercial fishing is prohibited.** NOAA’s sanctuary regulations prohibit commercial fishing and possession of commercial fishing gear unless it is stowed and unavailable for immediate use. The monument’s broader rules also prohibit taking or disturbing resources unless authorized by a monument permit. [NOAA sanctuary regulations](https://sanctuaries.noaa.gov/papahanaumokuakea/management/regulations.html); [NOAA fishing-impact overview](https://sanctuaries.noaa.gov/science/sentinel-site-program/papahanaumokuakea/fishing-impacts.html).

**There are no-take protections across the monument, but fishing rules differ in the newly designated outer sanctuary area.** In the monument, fishing is generally prohibited unless permitted. In the Outer Sanctuary Zone—waters from 50 nautical miles to the U.S. EEZ boundary west of 163° W—non-commercial fishing may be allowed under applicable federal rules, provided the catch does not enter commerce; it requires authorization. Commercial fishing remains prohibited there. [NOAA sanctuary regulations](https://sanctuaries.noaa.gov/papahanaumokuakea/management/regulations.html).

So, describing the *entire* area as strictly no-take without qualification would miss the outer-zone allowance for authorized non-commercial fishing.

# IRON LADY — medium risk lead
**Summary:** The IRON LADY, a USA-flagged fishing vessel, apparently turned off its AIS tracking device while in the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument, a protected area where commercial fishing is prohibited. The vessel's tracking was off for 347 hours, during which it moved about 951 km.
## What happened
* 2026-07-10T16:10:17.000Z: AIS tracking turned off
* 2026-07-25T02:42:48.000Z: AIS tracking turned back on
## Why it matters
The IRON LADY's AIS tracking was switched off 1 time in a protected area, it had a long dark period of 347 hours, it moved 951 km while its tracking was off, and it has a repeat pattern of 3 tracking gaps in the previous 12 months, resulting in a risk score of 55.
## Vessel background
The IRON LADY is a fishing vessel flagged in the USA, owned by BOSTON SWORD AND TUNA, and has an MMSI of 367514890 and callsign WDG2365. In the 12 months prior to the incident, it had 3 tracking gaps, 15 fishing events, 0 encounters, 9 loitering events, and 14 port visits.
## What public sources say
The IRON LADY is identified as a fishing vessel registered in the United States, with no reported citations for IUU fishing, sanctions, detentions, or fines [1]. Commercial fishing is prohibited in the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument, with some exceptions for non-commercial fishing in the Outer Sanctuary Zone under applicable federal rules [9].
## What we don't know
None.
## Suggested next steps
1. Review the vessel's AIS data for the surrounding period to check for any other suspicious activity.
2. Investigate the vessel's fishing permits and licenses to determine if it was authorized to fish in the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument.
3. Check for any other reports or records of the IRON LADY's activities in the protected area.

mpa_rules.answer:
**Yes—industrial/commercial fishing is prohibited.** NOAA’s sanctuary regulations prohibit commercial fishing and possession of commercial fishing gear unless it is stowed and unavailable for immediate use. The monument’s broader rules also prohibit taking or disturbing resources unless authorized by a monument permit. [NOAA sanctuary regulations](https://sanctuaries.noaa.gov/papahanaumokuakea/management/regulations.html); [NOAA fishing-impact overview](https://sanctuaries.noaa.gov/science/sentinel-site-program/papahanaumokuakea/fishing-impacts.html).

**There are no-take protections across the monument, but fishing rules differ in the newly designated outer sanctuary area.** In the monument, fishing is generally prohibited unless permitted. In the Outer Sanctuary Zone—waters from 50 nautical miles to the U.S. EEZ boundary west of 163° W—non-commercial fishing may be allowed under applicable federal rules, provided the catch does not enter commerce; it requires authorization. Commercial fishing remains prohibited there. [NOAA sanctuary regulations](https://sanctuaries.noaa.gov/papahanaumokuakea/management/regulations.html).

So, describing the *entire* area as strictly no-take without qualification would miss the outer-zone allowance for authorized non-commercial fishing.

The latest information provided (through September 2026) concerns **proposed fishing access and regulation—not reports of illegal fishing or vessel detentions inside or near Papahānaumokuākea**. No recent detention or confirmed illegal-fishing incident is reported in these sources.

- **June 11, 2026:** President Trump signed a proclamation seeking to allow U.S.-flagged commercial fishing in parts of Papahānaumokuākea, including the Mau and Ho‘omalu zones and areas beyond 50 nautical miles. The move was criticized by conservation groups; the supplied material does not establish whether fishing has begun there.
- **September 16, 2026:** The Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council discussed fishing access and management for the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands and Papahānaumokuākea sanctuary, but deferred action on relevant regulations. It noted that other federal requirements—such as permits, reporting, catch limits, gear rules, monitoring and protected-species measures—would still apply.
- **Background:** One source reports that commercial fishing was briefly allowed in part of Papahānaumokuākea in an earlier period and cites NOAA data showing 7,800 sharks caught as bycatch in the last year fishing was allowed there. This is not a report of illegal fishing or a recent vessel detention.

**Bottom line:** The supplied news points to a contested effort to expand commercial fishing access, but it contains no confirmed recent report of illegal fishing or vessel detentions in or near the monument.

# Unidentified vessel (MMSI 368926671) — low risk lead
**Summary:** The Unidentified vessel (MMSI 368926671) was apparently loitering in the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument - Marine Protected Area on two occasions in late October 2026, raising concerns due to its unknown identity and activity. The vessel's presence in the protected area, where commercial fishing is prohibited, warrants further investigation.

## What happened
* 2026-10-27T19:26:24.000Z: Started loitering at 23.8533, -166.2892
* 2026-10-28T21:21:56.000Z: Ended loitering
* 2026-10-28T22:31:37.000Z: Started loitering again at 23.7825, -166.2125
* 2026-10-29T03:16:18.000Z: Ended loitering

## Why it matters
The vessel's risk score is 20, indicating a low risk level, due to reasons including loitering with another vessel at sea (possible catch transfer) and inability to identify the vessel in Global Fishing Watch registries or AIS records.

## Vessel background
The vessel is flagged as USA, but its identity, owner, and 12-month activity are partially unknown. In the 12 months prior to the event, it had 0 gap, 0 fishing, 0 encounter, 15 loitering, and 5 port visits recorded.

## What public sources say
Commercial fishing is prohibited in the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument [5][6][8]. Recent news reports indicate that there were discussions and proposals regarding fishing access and regulations in the area, but no specific reports of illegal fishing or vessel detentions were found [9][10][11].

## What we don't know
The vessel's owner and flag history are unknown due to its absence in Global Fishing Watch records.

## Suggested next steps
1. Verify the vessel's identity and ownership through other maritime databases or registries.
2. Investigate the vessel's activity before and after the loitering events to determine if it was engaged in fishing or other suspicious behavior.
3. Review AIS data for the vessel's movements and potential interactions with other vessels in the area.

mpa_rules.answer:
Fishing is prohibited throughout the Revillagigedo National Park—not just industrial or commercial fishing, but recreational fishing as well. The park is therefore a **no-take area**; the available information does not describe separate internal no-take zones or fishing-permitted zones.

**Official-source caveat:** The cited materials report that the 2017 presidential decree bans fishing, but they do not include the decree’s text or a Mexican government webpage. The IUCN account describes the decree as banning fishing in the reserve and on the islands. ProtectedSeas lists park rules prohibiting hunting and fishing, while pointing to the decree and 2019 management plan. These support the park-wide ban, but are not themselves Mexican government sources.

regional_news.answer:
The latest reported developments are from **July 2026**:

- On **July 7**, Mexico’s environment ministry (Semarnat), through CONANP, said it was designing an inter-agency strategy to combat illegal fishing in Revillagigedo National Park. The plan includes technological monitoring and coordination with Profepa, Conapesca, the federal prosecutor’s office, the Navy and the foreign ministry.
- A **July 9 report** said satellite monitoring had identified vessels that allegedly switched off their Automatic Identification System to enter the protected area undetected. It also noted that fishing has been prohibited within the park since its designation as a protected area in 2017.
- Earlier, in **April 2025**, CONANP reportedly used Skylight and Global Fishing Watch to detect a vessel suspected of illegal fishing near Clarión Island.

The material describes surveillance and enforcement plans, but **does not report a recent vessel detention or seizure** in or near the park.

# MADEIRA — low risk lead
**Summary:** The Mexican-flagged fishing vessel MADEIRA was detected loitering in the Revillagigedo National Park on 2026-06-24 for 2.05 hours, raising concerns about potential catch transfers. MADEIRA has a history of fishing and loitering activities in the area.
## What happened
* 2026-06-24T16:55:08.000Z: MADEIRA started loitering in Revillagigedo National Park
* 2026-06-24T18:58:12.000Z: MADEIRA ended loitering
## Why it matters
MADEIRA's loitering in a protected area, combined with its history of fishing activities, scored 10 for risk due to a possible catch transfer.
## Vessel background
MADEIRA is a Mexican-flagged fishing vessel (MMSI: 345080058, IMO: 7018991) authorized by IATTC. In the 12 months prior to the event, it had 119 fishing events, 4 encounters, 116 loitering events, and 9 port visits. Its owner is unknown.
## What public sources say
Fishing is prohibited throughout the Revillagigedo National Park [6]. In July 2026, Mexico's environment ministry announced an inter-agency strategy to combat illegal fishing in the park, including technological monitoring [9][11].
## What we don't know
None listed.
## Suggested next steps
1. Review MADEIRA's AIS data for the loitering event to determine if it was transmitting its position correctly.
2. Check if MADEIRA has any other recorded encounters or fishing activities near the Revillagigedo National Park.
3. Investigate MADEIRA's port visit to MAZATLAN on 2026-06-26 to determine if any cargo was offloaded.

mpa_rules.answer:
**Fishing is restricted by zone; it is not prohibited throughout the entire area.**

- **Zone 1 is a no-extraction marine reserve.** MiAmbiente says it covers about two-thirds of the water area and the entire seabed, and is for total protection and non-extraction of natural resources. Its plan prohibits commercial and sport fishing from boats, as well as listed fishing methods including trawls, nets, longlines, and other gear. [MiAmbiente: fishing licenses under the management plan](https://miambiente.gob.pa/licencias-de-pesca-para-caneros-se-realizaran-bajo-las-normas-establecidas-en-el-plan-de-manejo-de-la-zona-marina-protegida-de-coiba/); [Zone 1 summary of the management plan](https://map.navigatormap.org/site-detail?site_id=20418).
- **Zone 2 allows limited fishing under the plan’s rules.** MiAmbiente describes it as about 22,626 km² and says fishing with rod and line (“cañeros”) is subject to specific requirements. Thus, the available official information does **not** support saying that all commercial fishing is banned across the whole managed area. [MiAmbiente](https://miambiente.gob.pa/licencias-de-pesca-para-caneros-se-realizaran-bajo-las-normas-establecidas-en-el-plan-de-manejo-de-la-zona-marina-protegida-de-coiba/).
- MiAmbiente also states that restrictions on specified fishing gear remain in force throughout the area under Executive Decree 138 of June 8, 2021. [MiAmbiente: fishing must follow strict sustainability rules](https://miambiente.gob.pa/navarro-la-pesca-tiene-que-darse-bajo-normas-estrictas-de-sostenibilidad/).

**Bottom line:** There is a substantial no-take zone—Zone 1—but the supplied sources describe regulated fishing in Zone 2. The cited MiAmbiente pages are official; the detailed Zone 1 summary is hosted by ProtectedSeas Navigator, not an official government site.
